abstract: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) inhibit ice growth by binding to specific ice surfaces, although the molecular basis of this activity remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the ice-growth inhibition mechanism of the calcium-dependent antifreeze protein MaIBP_RIV from Marinomonas arctica using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations. MaIBP_RIV exhibits stable binding to the primary prism and basal ice planes through its ice-binding surface (IBS), effectively suppressing ice growth. IBS binding to the secondary prism plane is weaker and only temporarily inhibits growth. In contrast, the non-ice-binding surface (non-IBS) is repelled by the growing ice front. Our results also explain that Ca2+; stabilises the IBS and essential for ice-growth inhibition, while removing Ca2+; reduces IBS flatness, which significantly impairs its ice-growth activity. Experimentally characterised mutations on IBS residues (S44Y, G63D, N65Y, and D87Y) result in continuous ice growth, consistent with their reduced antifreeze activity. Hydration analysis of water molecules around IBS and non-IBS suggests that, by decreasing the temperature from 300K to 240K, the water molecules around IBS show more ice-like ordering compared to those around the non-IBS.
